drills.q: Name and order Cosmos DB's five consistency levels and explain the RU cost cliff between them.
drills.a: Strong, Bounded Staleness, Session, Consistent Prefix, Eventual (strongest to weakest). Strong and Bounded Staleness require quorum reads from two replicas, costing 2x the RUs of Session/Consistent Prefix/Eventual, which read from a single replica.

drills.q: A Cosmos DB container partitioned by tenant_id starts rejecting writes for one large tenant. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: The tenant's logical partition hit the hard 20GB ceiling, which cannot be raised and cannot be split for a single key value. Fix: redesign the partition key for higher cardinality (e.g., composite key with tenant_id plus a time bucket or entity type) so no single logical partition grows unboundedly.

drills.q: Compare Cosmos DB's consistency model to DynamoDB's and explain the specific trap for AWS engineers.
drills.a: DynamoDB offers a free binary per-request toggle (eventual vs strong consistent reads). Cosmos DB offers five distinct, database-configurable-with-per-request-override levels, and two of them (Strong, Bounded Staleness) carry a real 2x RU cost -- AWS engineers often assume a simple two-way toggle exists and miss both the three intermediate levels and the cost structure.

drills.q: Design the consistency strategy for inventory decrement, order placement confirmation, and a recently-viewed-items feed in an e-commerce system.
drills.a: Inventory decrement: Strong (or tight Bounded Staleness) -- overselling is a correctness bug worth the 2x RU cost. Order placement confirmation: Session -- read-your-own-writes is exactly what's needed at 1x RU. Recently-viewed feed: Eventual -- staleness is imperceptible, cheapest and lowest latency.

drills.q: Explain the architectural difference between Azure SQL Hyperscale and Business Critical, and when each wins.
drills.a: Hyperscale separates compute from distributed remote storage (page servers), up to 128TB, near-instant snapshot backups. Business Critical uses local SSD-backed synchronous replicas for lowest write commit latency but caps storage far lower (~4-16TB). Hyperscale wins for growth-uncertain/large workloads; Business Critical wins when sub-millisecond write latency matters more than storage ceiling.

drills.q: A team needs FIFO ordering and dead-letter handling for a queue. Why is Queue Storage wrong, and what should they use?
drills.a: Queue Storage has no FIFO guarantee and no built-in dead-lettering -- it's the simple/cheap option (64KB messages, basic polling, ~SQS Standard). Service Bus provides FIFO via sessions, built-in DLQ, and topics/subscriptions -- the correct choice whenever ordering or DLQ semantics are actual requirements.

drills.q: Why is PostgreSQL Single Server deprecated, and what should a migrating team plan for?
drills.a: Flexible Server superseded it with VNet-native networking and zone-redundant HA that Single Server lacked. Migration planning needs VNet/private-networking reconfiguration, a maintenance window (not automatically zero-downtime without explicit logical replication), and re-validation of extensions/config flags that may differ between deployment models.

drills.q: Explain Bounded Staleness's K-versions-or-T-time bound and give a scenario where it beats both Strong and Session.
drills.a: Bounded Staleness guarantees every reader across every region sees writes in the same order, lagging by at most K versions or T time -- a strictly global ordering guarantee Session doesn't provide (Session only orders within one client's session). It wins for scenarios like a cross-region leaderboard/auction needing consistent bounded-lag ordering across all readers without paying full cross-region synchronous Strong consistency's write latency.

drills.q: Design a Cosmos DB partition key for a multi-tenant SaaS system with tenant sizes ranging from tiny to enormous.
drills.a: A pure tenant_id key risks large tenants hitting the 20GB logical-partition ceiling. Use a composite/synthetic key (tenant_id plus a coarse time bucket or entity-type suffix) to spread a large tenant's data across multiple logical partitions, accepting that tenant-scoped queries now fan out across a known, bounded set of synthetic-key variants.

drills.q: A read-heavy Cosmos DB analytics dashboard is consuming far more RUs than expected. What do you investigate first?
drills.a: Check whether the read path inherited a Strong or Bounded Staleness default (2x RU multiplier with no benefit for staleness-tolerant analytics), and check for cross-partition queries lacking a partition key filter, which fan out to every physical partition and multiply RU cost by partition count. Moving to Eventual consistency and adding partition-key-filtered queries are the two highest-leverage fixes.

drills.q: Compare Cosmos DB's built-in partitioning to sharding PostgreSQL with Citus for a workload outgrowing a single instance.
drills.a: Cosmos DB partitioning is first-class and transparent within the document model (subject to the 20GB/10,000 RU/s per-logical-partition constraints). Citus-sharded PostgreSQL requires deliberately redesigning the schema around a distribution column, ensuring joins collocate on it, and accepting some relational features/query patterns work differently across shards -- a real, non-trivial redesign cost that should be weighed against the workload's existing relational investment.
